source_text: Et tamen, fratres mei, non inuidemus concordiae eorum. inter se suscitata odia diabolica finierunt, quomodo putant, in pacem redierunt. sed hoc dico: si ramus fractus quaesiuit paruum a se fractum, qua diligentia debet arbor ipsa quaerere ramum ex se fractum? ideo sudamus, ideo laboramus, ideo inter eorum arma et cruentas furias circumcellionum periclitati sumus et adhuc reliquias eorum qualicumque donata a deo patientia toleramus, dum arbor quaerit ramum, dum grex ex ouili Christi ouem perditam quaerit. si pastoralibus uisceribus praediti sumus, per saepes et spinas nos coartare debemus. membris. laceratis ouem quaeramus et pastori principique omnium cum laetitia reportemus. multa diximus etiam fatigati, et tamen frater noster, propter quem ista dicimus uobis et cui pariter dicimus et pro quo tanta agimus, adhuc pertinax sistit. constantem se putat fortitudo crudelis. non adhuc de uana et falsa fortitudine glorietur. audiat apostolum dicentem: uirtus in infirmitate perficitur. oremus pro illo. unde scimus quid uelit deus? multae cogitationes, sicut scriptum est, in corde uiri; consilium autem domini manet in aeternum.
thought_title: The tree seeks its broken branch
orientation: Augustine is addressing the gathered congregation at the end of the proceedings, urging them to see the Donatists' reconciliation among themselves as a sign of how much more the Catholic Church should seek the return of Emeritus.
pass_a_gloss: And yet, my brothers, we do not begrudge their concord. They ended the diabolical hatreds stirred up among themselves, they returned to peace, as they think. But this I say: if a broken branch sought a small branch broken from itself, with what diligence ought the tree itself to seek the branch broken from itself? Therefore we sweat, therefore we labor, therefore we have been endangered among their weapons and the bloody furies of the Circumcellions, and still we endure their remnants with whatever patience has been given by God, while the tree seeks the branch, while the flock seeks the lost sheep from the fold of Christ. If we are endowed with pastoral bowels, we ought to press ourselves through hedges and thorns. With torn limbs let us seek the sheep and bring it back with joy to the shepherd and prince of all. We have said many things even though wearied, and yet our brother, for whose sake we say these things to you and to whom we say them equally and for whom we do so much, still stands stubborn. Cruel strength thinks itself steadfast. Let him not glory any longer in empty and false strength. Let him hear the apostle saying: strength is made perfect in weakness. Let us pray for him. How do we know what God wants? Many thoughts, as it is written, are in the heart of a man; but the counsel of the Lord remains forever.

choices.why: Keeps the possessive force of eorum and the noun concordia as a state of agreement, matching Augustine's concessive tone.
Preserves the adjective as a quality of the hatreds, not a genitive of origin, and keeps the plural.
Keeps the participle as an attributive adjective and the indefinite article to match the rhetorical question's generalizing force.

choices.english: the bloody furies of the Circumcellions
choices.why: Uses the glossary term Circumcellions and keeps the genitive of source, preserving the violent imagery.
rejected: the bloody rages of the Circumcellions

choices.why: Keeps the anatomical metaphor literally, as Augustine uses uiscera for deep compassion; 'bowels' preserves the bodily image.
Keeps the noun-adjective order and the paradox of strength that is actually cruelty, matching Augustine's critique of Emeritus's stubbornness.

bible_refs.note: multae cogitationes in corde uiri; consilium autem domini manet in aeternum

pass_b_english: And yet, my brothers, we do not begrudge them their concord. They brought to an end the diabolical hatreds they had stirred up among themselves, and returned to peace, as they think. But this is what I say: if a broken branch went looking for a small branch broken from itself, with what care should the tree itself seek the branch broken from itself? That is why we sweat, why we labor, why we have been endangered amid their weapons and the bloody furies of the Circumcellions, and why we still endure their remnants with whatever patience God has given us—while the tree seeks its branch, while the flock seeks the lost sheep from Christ's fold. If we are endowed with pastoral bowels, we must press ourselves through hedges and thorns. With torn limbs, let us seek the sheep and carry it back with joy to the shepherd and ruler of all. We have said much, even though we are weary, and yet our brother—for whose sake we say these things to you, and to whom we say them equally, and for whom we do so much—still stands stubborn. Cruel strength thinks itself constancy. Let him no longer glory in empty and false strength. Let him hear the apostle say: "Power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Let us pray for him. How do we know what God wills? Many are the thoughts in a man's heart, as it is written, but the counsel of the Lord remains forever (Psalm 33:11 (LXX 32:11)).

problems.quote: returned to peace as they saw fit
problems.why: "quomodo putant" modifies how they think the hatreds ended, not how they returned to peace; "putant" = "as they think" or "in their view"
problems.fix: and returned to peace, as they think, having ended them

problems.quote: With torn limbs let us seek the sheep
problems.why: "membris laceratis" = with torn/maimed limbs (our own), but the English could imply tearing the sheep's limbs; also "laceratis" is passive (torn), not active
problems.fix: With our limbs torn, let us seek the sheep

edits.old: and returned to peace as they saw fit.
edits.new: and returned to peace, as they think.

edits.old: With torn limbs let us seek the sheep
edits.new: With our limbs torn, let us seek the sheep

fixed: Changed 'returned to peace as they saw fit' to 'returned to peace, as they think' because 'quomodo putant' modifies how they think the hatreds ended, not how they returned to peace.
Changed 'With torn limbs' to 'With our limbs torn' because 'membris laceratis' refers to our own torn limbs, not the sheep's, and is passive.

problems.why: "Membris" is dative/ablative with "laceratis" (torn limbs), but "ouem quaeramus" is jussive subjunctive; the English makes limbs the subject's own, but Latin is absolute or instrumental.
problems.fix: our limbs torn, let us seek the sheep

problems.source_quote: multae cogitationes, sicut scriptum est, in corde uiri; consilium autem domini manet in aeternum
problems.why: The Latin matches Psalm 32:11 (LXX/Vulgate) or Proverbs 19:21 partially, but "manet in aeternum" is closer to Psalm 32:11 ("consilium autem eius manet in aeternum"); Proverbs 19:21 has "consilium Domini stabit." The citation is questionable.
problems.ruling: Proverbs 19:21 has 'consilium Domini stabit'; 'manet in aeternum' matches Psalm 32:11, wrong reference.

edits.old: With our limbs torn, let us seek the sheep
edits.new: With torn limbs, let us seek the sheep

fixed: Changed 'With our limbs torn' to 'With torn limbs' to reflect the Latin absolute/instrumental 'membris laceratis' without implying the limbs are the subject's own.
Changed the citation from Proverbs 19:21 to Psalm 33:11 (LXX 32:11), since 'consilium autem domini manet in aeternum' matches the Psalm wording more closely than Proverbs.

last_rejected.quote: They brought to an end the diabolical hatreds they had stirred up among themselves
last_rejected.source_quote: inter se suscitata odia diabolica finierunt
last_rejected.why: Subject is the hatreds, not 'they'; hatreds ended, people didn't end them.
last_rejected.fix: The diabolical hatreds stirred up among themselves came to an end
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'finierunt' has no expressed subject; 'they' is supplied naturally. Hatreds ending themselves is personification; translator reasonably supplies 'they' (the people) as agents.

last_rejected.why: "Viscera" means inward affection/compassion, not bowels; "bowels" is archaic but still absurd here.
last_rejected.ruling: Viscera literally means bowels; 'pastoral bowels' is archaic but within normal range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: press ourselves through hedges and thorns
last_rejected.source_quote: per saepes et spinas nos coartare debemus
last_rejected.why: "Coartare" means to confine/restrict oneself, not press through; the image is of squeezing through narrow gaps.
last_rejected.fix: we must squeeze ourselves through hedges and thorns
last_rejected.ruling: Coartare = press/constrain; 'press ourselves through' captures squeezing through hedges, acceptable rendering.

last_rejected.why: "Membris" is dative/ablative plural; "laceratis" modifies the implied "nobis" or describes the state of being wounded, not "with torn limbs" as object.
last_rejected.fix: With our members torn, let us seek the sheep
last_rejected.ruling: Membris laceratis ablative phrase; 'with torn limbs' correctly renders the ablative of circumstance/state.

last_rejected.quote: carry it back with joy to the shepherd and ruler of all
last_rejected.why: "Reportemus" means bring back/carry back; but "pastori principique omnium" is dative, and the joy goes with the action, but "ruler of all" obscures that this is Christ.
last_rejected.fix: bring it back with joy to the shepherd and prince of all
last_rejected.ruling: Reportemus = carry back; 'ruler of all' renders principi omnium; no meaning lost, Christ implied.

last_rejected.quote: to whom we say them equally
last_rejected.why: "Pariter" means equally/similarly, but here it means "we say to him as well" (to him too, not just to you), not "equally."
last_rejected.fix: and to him we also say them
last_rejected.ruling: Pariter can mean equally; 'say them equally' is within range, not a clear mistranslation.

last_rejected.why: "Sistit" means he stands still/remains; "pertinax" is obstinate, but "stands stubborn" connotes a posture, not persistence.
last_rejected.ruling: Sistit = stands/remains; 'stands stubborn' captures pertinax sistit adequately, no meaning change.
